reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO
clinicalPearls: Results from infection with group A streptococcus strains that produce erythrogenic (pyrogenic) exotoxins, usually complicating streptococcal pharyngitis and occasionally skin infection
Presents with sore throat, fever, and a diffuse fine erythematous rash with a sandpaper texture that blanches on pressure
The rash characteristically accentuates in skin folds (Pastia's lines) and spares the perioral area, giving circumoral pallor
The tongue shows a white coating that peels to reveal a red, swollen surface with prominent papillae described as a strawberry tongue
Desquamation of the skin, particularly of the fingertips and toes, follows as the rash fades over the ensuing days to weeks
Diagnosis rests on the clinical picture supported by throat swab culture or rapid antigen testing for group A streptococcus
Timely antibiotic treatment shortens illness, reduces spread, and lowers the risk of suppurative and non-suppurative complications, with penicillin-class agents as the mainstay
reference.pathophysiology: Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) strains lysogenised by bacteriophages produce streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins. In a host lacking antibody to the relevant toxin, these act as superantigens and toxins that cause the characteristic diffuse erythematous eruption and systemic features. The primary focus is usually the pharynx. Beyond the local infection, immune-mediated sequelae can follow, including acute rheumatic fever and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, and unchecked infection can extend to suppurative complications.
additionalDifferentials: Viral exanthems such as erythema infantum or enteroviral rash
infectionMimics: Staphylococcal scalded skin / toxic shock syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Throat swab for culture and/or rapid antigen detection of group A streptococcus
Anti-streptolysin O and other streptococcal antibody titres to confirm recent infection when needed
Urinalysis to screen for post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis in the convalescent phase
Inflammatory markers and basic bloods if a complicated or invasive infection is suspected
redFlags: Features of acute rheumatic fever such as migratory arthritis, carditis, or new murmur developing after the illness
Signs of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis including haematuria, oedema, and hypertension
Suppurative complications such as peritonsillar or retropharyngeal abscess, otitis media, or cervical lymphadenitis
Rapid deterioration with hypotension and multi-organ involvement suggesting streptococcal toxic shock syndrome or invasive disease
reference.prognosis: With prompt antibiotic therapy the outlook is excellent and most children recover fully; the main concern with untreated or inadequately treated disease is the risk of rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis, and suppurative spread.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis when the rash is faint or the pharyngitis mild, delaying treatment that prevents complications
Failing to complete the full antibiotic course, which is important for preventing rheumatic sequelae
Confusing scarlet fever with Kawasaki disease and overlooking coronary risk in a young child
Not monitoring for delayed post-streptococcal renal or cardiac complications after apparent recovery
management: Treat with a penicillin such as phenoxymethylpenicillin as first-line antibiotic therapy, using a macrolide for penicillin allergy
Complete the full antibiotic course to eradicate group A streptococcus and prevent rheumatic fever and suppurative complications
Provide supportive care with antipyretics, analgesia, and adequate fluid intake
Exclude the child from school or nursery until an appropriate interval after starting antibiotics to limit spread
Monitor during convalescence for post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and features of acute rheumatic fever
Notify public health authorities and consider treating symptomatic close contacts, particularly during outbreaks
